pages.x: About us An engineering company in Osaka, building dependable technology with care. Who we are Tenshi Systems Engineering is an engineering and technology company based in Osaka, Japan. We help organizations plan, build and run the systems they depend on, from custom software and websites to hosting, AI and branding. We believe good technology should be dependable, easy to understand and built to last. That is why we take time to listen, explain our choices clearly and stay involved long after launch. 天使 Our name Tenshi (天使) means “angel” in Japanese. For us it is a promise: to look after every project, and every client, with care, from the first conversation to long after launch. Our mission Our mission is to gain capital, design a large robot and then dominate the world bringing about peace and a long period of advanced industrialization and personal abundance. Our vision A web where every business, from a family shop in Osaka to a company working across continents, has a website that is well made, honest and quick for everyone who visits it. Our speciality: the web We offer nine services, but the web is where we spend most of our days. Design, development and hosting are three halves of the same job to us: a beautiful site is useless if it is slow, and a fast site is useless if it goes offline. We handle all three, so nothing falls between the cracks. Web design Design starts with your visitors, not with colours. We study who they are, what they came to do and what stops them, then plan the structure of every page as a sitemap and wireframes. Before any code is written you click through an interactive prototype on your own phone and computer, so ideas are tested early and changes cost little. Every layout is designed mobile-first and adapts smoothly to tablets and…

pages.x: Web Design Clean, responsive websites designed around your brand and your visitors, on every screen. Web Design Your website is often the first impression of your business. We design sites that are clear, welcoming, and easy to use on phones, tablets, and computers, with layouts built around what your visitors came to do. Who it's for Companies launching a new website, refreshing an outdated one, or improving how visitors find what they need. Deploy Your Future In depth Web Design shapes the experience visitors have the moment they arrive on your site. We start by understanding your audience and their goals, then plan the structure of every page, sketch wireframes and build interactive prototypes you can click through before anything is developed. This lets you test ideas early and change direction cheaply. The finished designs are responsive, so they look and work beautifully on phones, tablets and large screens. Here is how the main options differ and what to ask before you choose. Every website lives on a computer somewhere, connected to the internet around the clock. Web hosting is the service that provides that computer, keeps it running, and delivers your pages to visitors when they type in your address. It is easy to treat hosting as a commodity and pick the cheapest plan on offer. But the host you choose affects how fast your site loads, how often it is unavailable, how safe it is, and how much work it takes to keep it healthy. This guide explains the main types of hosting in plain English, what actually matters when comparing them, and the questions worth asking before you sign up or move. The Main Types of Hosting Most hosting falls into a handful of categories. The names vary from provider to provider, but the underlying ideas are consistent. Shared hosting. Your site sits on a server alongside many other websites, sharing its processing power, memory, and storage. It is inexpensive and usually comes with a simple control panel. The trade-off is that a busy or badly behaved neighbor can slow your site down, and you have limited control over the server's setup. Virtual private server (VPS). One physical machine is divided into several isolated virtual servers, and you get one of them with a guaranteed share of resources. That brings more consistent performance and more control, but someone has to configure, update, and secure that server. Cloud hosting. How to Choose the Right Foundation for Your Website Before a single page is designed, every website project faces a quiet but important decision: how will this site be built and managed? The answer shapes how fast your site loads, how easily your team can update it, how much it costs to maintain, and how exposed it is to security problems. Most business websites end up on one of two paths, a content management system (CMS) or a static site, with a growing middle ground between them. There is no universally right choice. There is only the right choice for how your business actually works. Here is how to think it through. Two Approaches, Explained Simply A traditional CMS such as WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla stores your content in a database. When someone visits a page, the server pulls content from the database, combines it with a template, and builds the page on the spot. You log in to an admin dashboard to edit text, add images, and publish posts. A static site is made of pre-built HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. The pages are assembled ahead of time, often by a tool called a static site generator such as Hugo, Eleventy, Jekyll, or Astro, and then uploaded to a server or hosting platform. When a visitor arrives, the server simply hands over a finished file. There is no database lookup and no page building in real time. The middle ground is a headless CMS. Services such as Contentful, Sanity, Strapi, or Decap CMS give editors a friendly interface for writing content, while the public website is generated as fast static pages. They might be on a train, standing in line, or comparing options on the couch. If your website was designed for a large desktop monitor and then squeezed down to fit a phone, they will feel it: tiny text, buttons that are hard to tap, and menus that fight back. Mobile-first design flips that process around. In this post, we explain what mobile-first and responsive design actually mean, why they matter for small and mid-size businesses, and how to check whether your own site measures up. Responsive Design and Mobile-First: What Is the Difference? These two terms are often used together, but they describe different ideas. Responsive design means a single website adapts its layout to the screen it is viewed on. Columns stack, images resize, and navigation changes shape, all from the same code and the same web address. Mobile-first is a way of working. Designers and developers plan the small-screen experience first, then add layout and features as more space becomes available. The order matters. When you start with a large screen, it is easy to fill space with extras that later have to be hidden or crammed onto a phone. When you start small, you are forced to decide what is truly important, and that clarity usually improves the desktop version too. Why Mobile-First Matters for Your Business A mobile-first approach is not just a technical preference. It affects how customers experience your brand and how search engines evaluate your site. On a website, text is the product: it is how visitors learn what you do, what it costs, and how to contact you. A few readability fundamentals apply to almost every site: Body text size: Around 16 pixels is a common baseline for body copy on screens, and larger is often better for content-heavy sites or older audiences. Alignment: Left-aligned text is usually easiest to scan in English. Fully justified text can create uneven gaps between words on the web. Or someone with a tremor who navigates with a keyboard instead of a mouse. Or an older visitor who simply needs larger, higher-contrast text. If your website works for them, it is accessible. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, are published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the organization that develops many core web standards. The current version is WCAG 2.2, released in October 2023. The guidelines are organized into three conformance levels: Level A: The minimum. Failing these makes content unusable for some people. Level AA: The level most organizations and many laws aim for. It covers the barriers that affect the largest number of users. Level AAA: The highest level, often not achievable for every type of content, and usually applied selectively. For most business websites, Level AA is the sensible target. In Japan, the national standard for web accessibility is JIS X 8341-3, which is aligned with WCAG. Before the First Field: Earning the Click People decide whether to fill out a form before they reach the first field. They are asking themselves two questions: is this worth my time, and can I trust this company with my information? Help them answer yes: Explain what happens next. "We will reply within one business day with a few questions about your project" is far more reassuring than a bare "Submit." State the benefit. Make clear what they will receive, whether that is a quote, a callback, a consultation, or a download. Show the effort upfront. A short form signals respect for their time. If a form must be long, say roughly how long it takes. Place forms where decisions happen. A contact option at the end of each service page catches people at the moment they are ready, rather than sending them hunting for a contact page. Offer alternatives. Some people prefer a phone call, email, or a messaging app. Providing options alongside the form keeps those visitors too. Ask for Less, Ask Clearly Every field is a small request. pages.x: Technology Nov 16, 2026 · 5 min read Website Analytics in Plain English: How to Tell If Your Site Is Doing Its Job A website can look fine and still miss its purpose. Here is how to read the numbers that show whether visitors find you, understand you, and get in touch. A website can look professional, load quickly, and still fall short of the job that matters: helping the right people understand what you offer and take the next step. Analytics will not fix that on its own, but it will show you what is actually happening, instead of what you hope is happening. This guide explains the idea in plain English, names the numbers that usually matter, and suggests a simple monthly habit you can keep. Analytics Is a Record of Behavior, Not a Scorecard Website analytics is a record of how people find your site and what they do while they are there. Typical tools show how many visits you received, which pages were opened, whether someone arrived from a search engine or a link, and whether they used a phone or a computer. That record is useful, but it is not a verdict on your brand, and it is not a sales report. Think of it as a flashlight: it helps you see patterns, not a crystal ball. One well-installed tool, a few clear goals, and a regular look at the results are enough for most small and mid-size businesses. The Numbers That Usually Matter Begin with questions you already have, not with a dashboard full of charts. Are people finding us? Which pages do they read? Do they get as far as contacting us? If a report does not help you answer those questions, you can usually ignore it, including vanity metrics such as raw page-view counts or follower totals that never turn into inquiries. pages.x: Security Nov 11, 2026 · 5 min read Website Security Essentials: A Practical Checklist for Small Businesses It is easy to assume that hackers only go after banks and large corporations. In reality, most attacks on websites are automated. Bots scan the internet around the clock looking for outdated software, weak passwords, and misconfigured servers. They do not care how big your company is; they care whether your site has an open door. A compromised website can show spam to your customers, redirect them to scam pages, leak form submissions, or be flagged by browsers as unsafe. The encouraging news is that a handful of consistent habits prevent the large majority of everyday problems. Think of website security not as one big lock, but as several layers, each one making the next attack harder. Layer One: Encrypt Everything With HTTPS HTTPS encrypts the connection between your visitor's browser and your website, so information like contact form entries and login details cannot be read or altered in transit. It relies on an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your server. What to check: Every page on your site loads with https:// , not just the checkout or contact page. Visitors who type http:// are automatically redirected to the secure version. Your certificate renews automatically. Free certificates from Let's Encrypt, offered by many hosts, typically renew every 90 days, and an expired certificate triggers alarming browser warnings. There is no "mixed content," meaning images or scripts still loading over plain HTTP. Modern browsers label non-HTTPS pages as "Not secure," so this layer protects your reputation as much as your data.
